<reason>CON (A) built the cleaner path to victory. A's core line—size is a static proxy that prices the object rather than the use—was introduced early, pressed consistently, and sharpened each round. A answered both pressure questions directly in proper A1:/A2: format, coherently distinguishing use-scaled cost recovery (tolls, weight fees) from a static surcharge sold as safety. The decisive moment was B's Rebuttal 2 pivot—"cost recovery alone justifies it; behavior change is the bonus"—which A caught and converted into a retreat narrative ("dead pedestrians quietly became a revenue argument") that B never repaired. A also correctly fixed B's misdescription of liability insurance, exposed the exemption-eats-the-rationale problem for curb fees, and closed with a damaging textual catch: B defended a sliding per-foot/per-pound scale while the motion as defended (weight/hood-height thresholds) enacts a category cliff, and the fee touches mass but never velocity, miles, or behavior. B had real strengths—a strong opening, the excellent "pure tax" reversal question, the clean big-with-AEB vs. small-with-AEB comparison, and a memorable "size is the cost" closing frame—but suffered a clipped Rebuttal 2, a premature "they never answered" claim that A then answered, and nonexistent reference IDs. B stayed competitive throughout, but A adapted better, answered pressure more honestly, and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1–A4.3): directly answered both pressure questions, then seized on B's "cost recovery alone justifies it" concession to reframe the entire safety case as a quietly abandoned revenue argument—a catch A rode through the closing and B never neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
